identity.title: DNA barcoding and cellular senescence in atherosclerosis: Vascular smooth muscle cell lineage tracing and potential for future Senotherapeutics.

content.abstract: Cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, and substantial risk persists even with optimal preventive therapy. Cellular senescence is a state of growth arrest accompanied by a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) and has emerged as a candidate driver of vascular disease states. Recently, vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) have moved from passive bystanders in vascular diseases, including atherosclerosis, to pivotal cells integral to many facets of plaque biology. Within the lesion microenvironment, VSMCs undergo phenotypic switching and de-differentiation into macrophage-like, osteogenic, fibromyocyte, and senescent states, frequently extinguishing canonical lineage markers. However, defining the independent contribution of senescent VSMCs is complicated by two converging problems: the absence of a universal, specific senescence marker, and the loss of identity that accompanies VSMC trans-differentiation. We argue that DNA barcoding, a high-resolution, marker-independent lineage-tracing strategy matured in hematology and oncology, can address both obstacles. Building on the established foundation of multicolor reporters, we contrast static high-diversity libraries with evolving CRISPR-Cas9 recorders and human-translatable retrospective approaches, emphasizing that barcoding reports clonal lineage and must be paired with single-cell and spatial transcriptomics to position the senescent state on a reconstructed clonal tree. We further appraise emerging senotherapeutics, whose inconsistent and occasionally harmful in vivo results reflect a failure to identify the target cell rather than a failure of pharmacology. This distinction argues for lineage-restricted targeting. Integrating clonal barcoding, spatial multi-omics, and senescence atlases may help resolve the role of VSMC senescence in atherogenesis and enable cell-state-specific therapy.
